description: Hack the Seas Village explores maritime cybersecurity, vessel navigation systems, Automatic Identification System (AIS) RF security, and autonomous underwater vehicle operations.

talks.title: Build a Raspberry AIS

talks.title: Hacker Challenge: Single Point Prediction
talks.teaser: Presents a maritime tracking challenge on analyzing vessel paths and predicting single-point coordinates from RF telemetry.
talks.summary:
In this data science session from the DEF CON Safe Mode Hack the Seas Village, the presenter introduces the "Single Point Prediction" challenge, exploring trajectory forecasting algorithms for maritime vessels. Opening at 00:00, the speaker details the challenge objective: predicting future vessel coordinates based on sparse, intermittent telemetry data.

At 04:02 and 08:01, the presentation breaks down Automatic Identification System (AIS) message formats, focusing on Class A position reports (Types 1, 2, and 3). The speaker shows how vessel speed, rate of turn, and navigation status can be modeled to predict vessel transit paths even through GPS dead zones.

Concluding at 12:00, the presenter reviews model scoring criteria and invites data scientists and maritime security researchers to develop predictive algorithms capable of identifying anomalous vessel behaviors and spoofed AIS tracks. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: AIS Spoofing Attacks and Some Tools
talks.teaser: Explores vulnerability vectors in unauthenticated maritime AIS protocols and demonstrates tools for detecting and simulating RF spoofing.
talks.summary:
Maritime cybersecurity researcher Dr. Gary Kessler demonstrates the mechanics of Automatic Identification System (AIS) spoofing attacks and introduces analytical tools to identify maritime positioning anomalies in the Hack the Seas Village [00:00].

Kessler breaks down the AIS radio frequency protocol and its integration with satellite constellations and vessel transponders [12:11, 36:45]. He analyzes real-world case studies of replay and geographic spoofing attacks—such as ghost vessels appearing at coordinates they occupied months prior [49:27]—explaining the absence of cryptographic authentication in global AIS broadcasts and showing how software-defined radios (SDRs) can manipulate commercial shipping tracking to evade sanctions or confuse collision-avoidance systems [01:03:13].

talks.title: Speed 2: The Poseidon Adventure
talks.teaser: Examines real-world cyber attack surfaces across cruise ships, maritime navigation systems, and onboard industrial controls.

Social Engineering and Human-Oriented Security

This presentation explores social engineering attacks and human vulnerability in security systems. Topics include psychological manipulation, pretexting, credential harvesting, and how attackers exploit human nature to bypass technical defenses.

talks.title: Yacht Pwned
talks.teaser: Uncovers vulnerabilities in luxury yacht automation systems, NMEA 2000 marine networks, and satellite telematics.
talks.summary:
In this technical penetration testing briefing from the DEF CON Safe Mode Hack the Seas Village, researcher OB166 presents "Yacht Pwned," exploring the expansive digital and industrial attack surface aboard luxury superyachts. Opening at 00:02, the speaker outlines the dense networking architectures deployed on modern mega-yachts.

At 12:00, he reveals that high-end vessels typically house multiple 42U equipment racks containing satellite communication modems, guest Wi-Fi infrastructure, entertainment servers, and marine automation controllers. At 24:01, the presenter demonstrates pivoting from unsegmented guest networks through NMEA gateways that bridge vessel IT with critical maritime operational networks.

At 36:02, he shows how sniffing unencrypted serial and Ethernet communications enables testers to manipulate environmental automation and navigation systems, concluding at 48:02 with defensive segmentation guidelines published on his maritime research repository. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: 40,000 Leagues UUV Death Match
talks.teaser: Analyzes the operational cybersecurity challenges, communication constraints, and vulnerability landscapes of unmanned underwater vehicles.
talks.summary:
Naval War College researcher Dr. Nina Kollars introduces the "40,000 Leagues UUV Death Match" challenge in the Hack the Seas Village, outlining the engineering hurdles and tactical realities of autonomous Unmanned Underwater Vehicles (UUVs) [00:00, 00:09].

The presentation details the physics of undersea operations, contrasting aerial drone communications with underwater signal propagation where RF and GPS fail entirely, leaving acoustic and optical signaling as the primary communication channels [11:18, 22:42]. Kollars examines naval operational doctrines, evasion tactics, and kinetic collision avoidance [33:35], detailing competition rules for building resilient, modular undersea drones capable of navigating adversarial aquatic environments [45:02].
